To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method was used to model carbon ablation using the new reactive scattering data from beam experiments.

molecular simulations of the interaction of oxygen with a carbon– carbon composite material can be used to predict the erosion rate and to determine the relative roles of gas–surface and gas–gas reactions for the erosion process.

(1) The reactive scattering experiments show that the surface reaction probabilities for the dissociation of molecular oxygen on a carbon surface are much higher than those reported in previous studies; (2) The molecular simulations show that the surface chemistry is dominated by the dissociation of the molecular oxygen, which is consistent with the results of the reactive scattering experiments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of chemical reactions at surfaces.
the development of a predictive model of the interaction of oxygen with the surface of a carbon–carbon ablator in a high-temperature environment.
the fundamental mechanisms of gas–surface chemical reactions at high temperatures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the molecular simulation approach, as presented here, is capable of reproducing the experimental results.
, in the present case, the surface reaction is the dominant mechanism, but the gas-phase chemistry plays a significant role.
, for the present conditions of interest, the gas phase is the major source for the CO2 production, while gas surface reactions are the major source of the CO production.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our work has shown that the gas-phase chemistry is very important and that the surface reaction probabilities can be determined using a molecular beam technique.
the molecular dynamics simulation is able to reproduce experimental results for the ablation of carbon materials by oxygen.
the simulations and the experiments have provided new information on the mechanisms for carbon ablation in high-temperature dissociative oxygen.

the surface chemistry and the microstructure are key factors in understanding ablation of carbon materials in high-temperature environments.
molecular simulations can be used to model the complex gas–surface interactions that occur during the ablation of carbon materials in high-temperature oxygen environments.
